title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
raw_text: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle. We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation. For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync. Across this shared model-state layer, TPU Sync integrates directly into existing infrastructure stacks across PyTorch (via TorchTPU ) and JAX — serving as the TPU KV cache connector for vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d disaggregated serving, while providing low-level transfer primitives for Pathways and multi-controller JAX (McJAX) RL pipelines. Understanding TPU Sync: The kitchen analogy To understand TPU Sync’s impact, imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen. Think of the TPU as an incredibly fast executive chef working on a tiny countertop (the chip's HBM). When preparing a massive feast, the chef needs lots of ingredients (the KV cache), which quickly clutter the counter. The standard kitchen (without TPU Sync): When the small counter fills up, the chef has to toss out prepped ingredients and chop them again from scratch the next time an order needs them — stalling the kitchen on repetitive prep work (prefill recomputation). The upgraded kitchen (with TPU Sync): TPU Sync adds a spacious side pantry (pinned host RAM), a shared walk-in cold storage room accessible to every station in the kitchen (shared cluster storage), and a coordinated team of runners. The runners slide full prep trays directly between the counter, the pantry, and peer stations without repacking them (direct DMA in native TPU layout). Crucially, the runners swap trays in and out while the chef keeps cooking (asynchronous, non-blocking transfers). Key use cases for TPU Sync TPU Sync improves system throughput and latency in workloads requiring deep context, high concurrency, multi-turn reasoning and RL rollouts: Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats : When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage). Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation. Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead. Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates. Breaking through the memory wall with TPU Sync At its core, TPU Sync establishes a high-performance data transfer path between TPU HBM and host RAM, as well as across TPU hosts via the DCN. It achieves this through four key architectural advantages: Layout-preserving direct DMA with in-place buffer aliasing : TPU Sync accesses the underlying JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place and moves slices directly between TPU HBM and page-locked ( DmaMap -registered) host memory in a single hardware DMA. By keeping tensors in their native TPU physical tile layout across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and the wire, data lands ready for immediate Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) execution with no Python serialization, no layout conversion, and no user-space bounce buffers. Compute-overlapped transfers : Rather than taking an exclusive lock or making an on-device copy of static KV cache and weight buffers, TPU Sync creates raw PJRT buffer aliases ( PJRT_RawBuffer ) without holding PJRT usage locks so block-level transfers can run concurrently with active in-place computation, with built-in DMA pacing to keep large transfers from delaying kernel launches. No XLA compilation in the data path : Because TPU Sync executes transfers and tile-aware strided resharding in native C++ outside the XLA graph, moving KV blocks or resharding weights across different trainer and sampler topologies does not trigger runtime compilation — keeping the data path fast and framework-agnostic. High-bandwidth PCIe DMA and DCN streaming : Using the raw_transfer library’s direct PJRT raw-buffer DMA pipeline, TPU Sync reaches up to 223 GB/s of aggregate D2H and H2D throughput per Ironwood (TPU v7x) host out of the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 hardware ceiling, and streams across the DCN at up to ~192 Gbps on a single 200 Gbps NIC (or ~350 Gbps across dual 200 Gbps NICs with NUMA-aware multi-NIC striping). TPU Sync exposes a low-level data transfer API, making it easier for developers to integrate high-speed TPU data transfer into higher-level frameworks. Higher-level architecture Built on top of its core transport and resharding primitives, TPU Sync provides a modular orchestration stack for distributed cache management: Global KV store: A global registry that maps prompt prefix hashes to physical cache blocks, handles dynamic lookups, and coordinates LRU eviction and tier demotion. TPU Sync controller: The orchestration layer that generates transfer plans, coordinates data movement across nodes, and handles lease management and recovery. KV cache manager: The local execution engine that tracks block states, manages HBM, host DRAM (including /dev/shm warm-boot persistence) alongside experimental POSIX storage backends, and executes asynchronous DMA transfers. Figure 1. TPU Sync operates as the model-state layer on TPU, unifying TPU HBM (Tier 1), pinned host DRAM (Tier 2), shared storage (Tier 3), and multi-host DCN under a single layout-preserving DMA data plane. Solving disaggregated serving and prefix caching Let us take a closer look at how TPU Sync helps with some of the use cases we listed in the earlier section. By treating host pinned memory as a substantial, high-speed Tier 2 cache, TPU Sync reduces the fragmentation and memory limits of standard HBM setups. Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregated serving In state-of-the-art serving topologies, prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases are isolated on separate node pools. To prevent latency bubbles, TPU Sync bridges this gap with a highly optimized, three-step pipeline: Direct-DMA offloading: Once a prefill node processes an initial prompt, TPU Sync immediately moves the resulting KV blocks into pinned host RAM via its asynchronous D2H DMA path. Host-to-host streaming : The TPU Sync controller then orchestrates a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) transfer, streaming the context directly to the assigned decode node. Overlapped ingestion : As blocks arrive in the decode node's host RAM, TPU Sync triggers an asynchronous H2D transfer directly into TPU HBM. This happens concurrently with active decoding computation, substantially minimizing TTFT. Host-powered prefix caching For highly concurrent systems sharing large system prompts or running multi-turn agentic loops, TPU HBM is not large enough to hold multiple active cache blocks. TPU Sync extends the prefix cache out of HBM (Tier 1) into substantial, distributed host RAM pools (Tier 2). Because TPU Sync transfers are asynchronous, it overlaps the PCIe DMA loading of the next required prefix from host RAM with the compute of the current request — minimizing TPU idle time between requests. For workloads that exceed even host DRAM capacity, TPU Sync also includes an experimental POSIX storage backend (Tier 3+) that asynchronously spills older KV blocks to local SSDs or shared Google Cloud Managed Lustre storage — pairing with llm-d prefix-affinity routing on GKE so replicas can recall cached prefixes across tiers without recomputing prompts. Sample performance results P/D disaggregated inference result highlights: Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut : For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms. Substantial TTFT reduction : Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency. Substantial high-traffic scalability : During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution. Prefix caching result highlights: Expands KV cache capacity beyond HBM : When heavyweight MoE model weights consume most of device HBM, on-chip memory can hold only a few long-context prefixes. Offloading into pinned host DRAM expands effective cache capacity by an order of magnitude. Sustains high cache-hit rates under concurrency : Pooling distributed host RAM keeps shared system prompts and multi-turn agent contexts warm across thousands of concurrent sessions instead of thrashing HBM. Significantly reduces prefill recompute : Directly bypasses heavy compute layers for repeated instruction blocks and system prompts, reducing average TTFT by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads while delivering over 50% higher throughput and a 30% reduction in P99 inter-token latency (ITL). Please see the note 1 below on the testing configuration. Ecosystem adoption and partnerships TPU Sync serves as the open, composable memory substrate across our PyTorch-on-TPU and Kubernetes serving ecosystem, built in close collaboration with key open-source maintainers and infrastructure partners: Inferact (vLLM-TorchTPU) : Co-engineered with Inferact, maintainers of vLLM-TorchTPU , TPU Sync is integrated directly via vLLM's native KVConnector interface. It powers Direct-DMA host DRAM offloading and multi-host P/D disaggregation across frontier open-source models. RadixArk (SGLang-TorchTPU) : In partnership with RadixArk, maintainers of SGLang-TorchTPU , TPU Sync serves as both the high-speed P/D disaggregation transfer backend and the native I/O backend for SGLang’s hierarchical cache. llm-d 1.0 integration : llm-d 1.0 pairs with TPU Sync on GKE to deliver global prefix-cache-affinity routing, per-rank decode session pinning, and experimental two-stage capacity spill to Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Get started TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch ( tpu-sync-torch ) and JAX ( tpu-sync-jax ), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU , SGLang-TorchTPU , and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides. We are committed to working with the open-source community to advance the model-state layer on TPU — supporting new frontier architectures, expanded storage tiering, and longer-horizon agentic and RL workloads. For more up-to-date performance results, please see our ongoing efforts on public benchmarks ( InferenceX ). 1. Performance results are based on internal testing conducted in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1 topology), configured with PCIe Gen5 (x16) per TPU chip and one or two 200 Gbps NICs enabled per host, running tpu-inference v0.24.0 (using JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1). Metrics presented represent average and median performance improvements observed under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual real-world performance, cache hit rates, and latency reductions will vary based on system configuration, network bandwidth, concurrent traffic, and specific user workload patterns.
summary: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle. We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

title: Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
raw_text: Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning. To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency. Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams: Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted. Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment. Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable. Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes. Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling. Dynamic slicing architecture GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube. Dynamic super-slicing GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency. Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice. How a 4x4x16 super slice (comprising 64 Ironwood VMs and 256 total chips) is formed using four Ironwood cubes (also provisioned as GKE nodepools). At runtime, the slice is created dynamically by stitching together the TPU network across all TPU chips in these four cubes. Dynamic sub-slicing Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy. When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool. How GKE sub-slicing dynamically partitions a 16-host TPU cube into smaller, independent slices (e.g., 2x2x4 with 16 chips down to 2x2x2) for optimal utilization of TPU resources. Customer use cases You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments. Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation . Getting started Pre-provision nodepools To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand. Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover. This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes. Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations. Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples. Repair When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies: Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes. Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions. Next steps Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation .

title: Our newest TPUs: 8tx and 8i Max, built for the agentic era
raw_text: Editor’s note: This blog was originally published on News from Google . We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more. At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. Today, we’re taking that a step further , expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference . This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max. While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads. The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements , our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. Building the computer around the chip Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer , so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years. The Future of AI Infrastructure Specializing for secure, high-context AI Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips: TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale. TPU 8tx TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with custom AMD CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters. Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution. TPU 8i Max Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall. When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt. The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density. While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack. Opening up TPUs to every developer When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code. Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware. This investment comes together today across these key areas: Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU , so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs. Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks: In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks , which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further. Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our accelerators more power-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends idle agent sessions and shifts working memory off the chip in milliseconds, cutting operational infrastructure costs. Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer ( TPU Sync ): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync , the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%. Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils , you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding. Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs. Co-designing with a decade of experience Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side. Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator. Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT.

title: Cloud Pathways, a distributed ML runtime for massive accelerator fleets, now GA
raw_text: Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways ( Pathways on Cloud ) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer . Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations. With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. We are also pleased to announce a Preview integration with Cluster Director to extend Cloud Pathways to Slurm clusters, supporting unified multi-slice JAX execution, elastic training, and interactive notebooks. What is Cloud Pathways? As AI workloads scale across thousands of accelerators, spanning multi-slice pre-training, disaggregated inference, and multi-program reinforcement learning (RL) loops, traditional multi-controller setups become harder to program and manage. In default multi-controller JAX, every TPU host runs its own separate Python interpreter with only a localized view of its connected devices and executes the same SPMD program in lockstep, making heterogeneous MPMD workflows and cross-slice resource management complex and brittle. Cloud Pathways replaces multi-controller management with a unified single-controller architecture built on the open-source Interim Framework Runtime (IFRT) . By setting JAX_PLATFORMS=proxy with pathwaysutils , a single JAX client process views and orchestrates multiple large TPU slices, spanning thousands of TPU chips as if they were all connected locally. Learn more about Pathways in our latest deep-dive blog here. Core architectural innovations Cloud Pathways has the following features: Single-controller orchestration: In Cloud Pathways, a single controller manages graph evaluation, persistent Cloud Storage compilation caching, and asynchronous XLA HLO dispatch across TPU slices. Colocated Python sidecars: Client-side colocated Python sidecar containers (with shared-memory support) let you run compute-intensive Python logic such as distributed data loading and checkpointing directly on TPU hosts. Resilient and elastic training: Cloud Pathways decouples job survival from individual slice interruptions with elastic training ( pathwaysutils ) using host-memory snapshots to dynamically reshard training down to N-1 slices during hardware failures without crashing the client. Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode , or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service. Proven enterprise impact and customer momentum Frontier AI labs, quantitative research firms, and global consumer platforms have adopted Cloud Pathways to run mission-critical production workloads on GKE, including: Hyperscale multi-host inference: One of the world's largest consumer technology companies runs production batch and reinforcement learning (RL) inference on Cloud Pathways across tens of thousands of TPU v5p , Trillium (v6e) , and Ironwood (TPU7x) chips, consuming over 100 million chip-hours per quarter, and co-designed elasticity primitives with Google to expand into pre-training. Elastic pre-training and multi-host RL for scientific foundation models: Google Cloud customer ZenteiQ uses Cloud Pathways on GKE with Cluster Toolkit ( gcluster ), colocated Python sidecars, and host snapshotting to scale elastic pre-training ( MaxText ) and single-controller reinforcement learning ( MaxText + Tunix ) across multi-slice Trillium ( v6e ) clusters for its scientific foundation models. "Running multi-day pre-training and post-training jobs on high-cost accelerators requires reliable continuity through both unexpected hardware faults and planned maintenance windows. By running Cloud TPUs and MaxText with Cloud Pathways on the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer stack, ZenteiQ relies on a proven controller that monitors our TPU topology and dynamically re-meshes and resizes the workload whenever a chip or slice goes offline. Combining Pathways with host snapshotting in production pushes recovery time down to a minimum when disruptions occur, keeping our available TPU capacity fully utilized with very little stall time. Our ML engineers no longer have to spend their hours watching job health or managing manual restarts, and can stay focused on their research workloads." - Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, ZenteiQ Getting started with Cloud Pathways Cloud Pathways is generally available today in all Google Cloud regions supporting Cloud TPU v5e , TPU v5p , Trillium (TPU v6e) , and Ironwood (TPU 7x) on GKE, with versioned container images ( us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways ) supporting JAX 0.10.1+ . Cloud Pathways is also available in Preview on Slurm TPU clusters in Cluster Director . To start building with Cloud Pathways: Read the overview: Explore the Introduction to Pathways on Cloud in the AI Hypercomputer documentation. Deploy your cluster: GKE: Follow the step-by-step guide to Create a GKE cluster with Pathways using Cluster Toolkit ( gcluster ) or the gcloud CLI. Slurm: Deploy Pathways via Cluster Director using the step-by-step guide . Run your workloads: Dive into our production guides for Batch workloads , Interactive notebook mode , Resilient & elastic training , Multihost inference , Porting JAX workloads , and Troubleshooting .

title: The code and the court: Why your email security thinks like Napoleon
raw_text: In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point. Certainty has a cost. A codified system is only as current as its code. When the world produces something the code did not anticipate — a new technology, a new fraud — there is no statute to apply, and everyone waits for someone to write one. Your email security works exactly this way. That is the problem. Security by statute A signature is a statute. Someone observes an attack, writes a rule that describes it, and from that moment you are protected against that attack and its close relatives. It is fast, certain, and blind to anything the code has not been written to see. Signatures alone were never enough, so the industry made the code bigger. Anomaly detection and behavioral models are a thicker statute book, trained on what already happened and scoring how far a message deviates from it. More sophisticated than a signature, but not a different philosophy. A zero-day is a crime with no statute. The strongest evidence against codified defense is not the attack that fails a check. It is the attack that passes every one. When a supplier’s mailbox is compromised, the message arrives from a real domain, with valid credentials and earned reputation. Every check comes back clean because the infrastructure is genuine. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that breaches involving a third party now account for 48% of the total, up 60% in a single year. Authentication did exactly what it measures : it confirmed the letter came from who it said, and had no rule for whether it should be believed. The code was consulted. The code said valid. The message was a theft in progress. Attackers understand this. A codified defense is cheap to walk around. You do not break the code; you do something it was never written to cover. The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report put business email compromise losses above $3 billion in a single year, much of it carried by messages that broke no rule because no rule described them. The other tradition The English-speaking world chose a different system. Common law does not always wait for the legislature. A judge facing a situation no statute anticipated can reason from principle and precedent to a verdict. It adapts case by case. It is not simply a code that has to be rewritten. It is a court that knows how to weigh a new set of facts. That is the difference between detecting and reasoning. The fair objection is that a reasoning system also learns from the past. True. But there is a difference between matching a case to a stored pattern and applying a principle to a case you have never seen. A judge who has never encountered your particular dispute still knows how to weigh evidence. None of this means throwing out the code. Most mail is open and shut and should be settled that way in milliseconds. You keep the fast rule for the easy calls and save a full hearing for the contested ones. A court can also answer a question a code struggles with: why. A codified system can say “this matched” or “this deviated.” A verdict can cite its evidence: what the sender actually is, whether the relationship supports the request, what the message is asking for. You do not have to trust the reasoning. You check the evidence, because a ruling stands or falls on whether its facts hold up, not on the private thoughts of the judge. It is the opposite of a black box: a decision you can read, challenge, and overturn. None of this retreats from zero trust. Zero trust governs access, who gets in and what they can touch, and assumes nothing. This is about the verdict, whether a message is what it claims to be, and there the posture is not to presume guilt or innocence but to let the evidence decide. The court of last resort For the highest stakes matters, a mature legal system does not let the machinery decide alone. In security, some decisions belong with the person whose money is about to move. When a message asks for a wire, a change to vendor banking details or a payroll redirect, the right design does not render a silent verdict and hope. It escalates and asks the owner to approve the action itself. Reasoning handles the general docket. The human is the court of last resort, reserved for the decisions that deserve one. Match the process to the stakes. No analogy is perfect. Real judges in both traditions do more than this, and civil-law systems evolve through their own doctrine. The question worth ending on For most of this industry’s history, there was no choice, because machines could apply a code but could not weigh evidence and reason for a judgment. That is no longer true. There is a simple way to find out which system you are running. Ask your team how many attacks that reached a user came from infrastructure you already trust: a compromised vendor, a real account, a genuine DocuSign or Microsoft notification bent to a purpose it was never meant for. If that number is high, your defenses are not failing to enforce the code. They are enforcing it perfectly; against threats the code was never written to describe. So, the question is not whether your defenses are up to date. A code is always, by definition, up to date with yesterday. The question is whether your security is a code or a court, and whether it can rule on the case it has never seen, because that is the only case that was ever going to hurt you.
summary: In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point.

title: 7 tips for achieving defensive agility
raw_text: Defensive security agility reflects an organization’s potential to rapidly detect, adapt, and respond to evolving cyber threats and vulnerabilities without disrupting core operations. By abandoning static, rigid defense architectures, an agile defense plan emphasizes continuous iteration, automation, and cross-functional flexibility. Defensive agility allows cybersecurity teams to rapidly adapt and respond to evolving threats while minimizing business disruption, says Anant Adya, an executive vice president at business and technology consulting firm Infosys. “As attack surfaces expand, organizations must prioritize risk quantification and identify vulnerabilities to strengthen their security posture and improve their ability to recover from attacks that are inevitable.” Is your organization taking the steps needed to achieve a high degree of defensive agility? Read on to find out. 1. Establish a zero-trust baseline Achieving defensive agility should begin with a zero-trust approach that continuously verifies access across users, devices, and applications, Adya advises. “An effective zero-trust strategy must be embedded into an organization’s technology framework and business lifecycle in order to build resilience and foster an organization-wide security mindset.” As enterprises adopt AI, modernize applications, and operate across highly distributed environments, security must evolve from a protective afterthought into a business accelerant, Adya says. “By integrating zero trust into day-to-day operations and AI workflows, organizations can strengthen their ability to adapt to evolving threats while innovating faster, integrating acquisitions more securely, and scaling globally without accumulating architectural or operational debt.” 2. Modernize (and rationalize) your existing security infrastructure Many large organizations are struggling to keep pace with emerging challenges because their systems are incredibly complex or filled with old software, custom code, and a mixture of disconnected security tools that can hinder containment speed, says Sharon Chand, cyber defense and resilience leader at Deloitte. Chand advises CISOs to evaluate their existing infrastructure and technologies to consider how they’re currently responding to threats. Meanwhile, it’s important to streamline operations into a more integrated system. “Security organizations must also have access to AI-driven systems to detect and automate response to machine-speed attacks at the pace of adversaries,” she states. 3. Enlist AI where confidence is high and actions are reversible Randy Gross, CISO at training and certification organization CompTIA, recommends deciding in advance which defensive actions are safe enough to happen without placing a human in the middle. “Locking an account, killing a session, or isolating a device should already be automated when confidence is high and the action is easy to reverse,” he says. Review your strategy at least quarterly, but never equate a strategy review with operational governance, Gross warns. “In a medium-to-large enterprise, agents’ permissions and integrations may change frequently, so the guardrails around them must be continuous and automated,” he advises. “The CISO and team should also revisit their strategy when enough changes have been made to the point where risk has changed materially.” Gross adds: “The strategy shouldn’t be just to put more AI in the SOC; it should be to reduce the latency between finding a threat and doing something useful about it.” 4. Forego higher walls in favor of dynamic, structural resilience Defensive agility requires an enterprise system with the architectural capacity to absorb, isolate, and adapt to anomalous behavior without relying on human intervention, says Jatin Chopra, a senior software engineer at Microsoft. “It marks the transition from static perimeter defense — where you build higher walls — to dynamic, structural resilience where the environment itself constantly shifts to restrict threat propagation.” Using an approach with sufficient capacity also detaches security from manual bottlenecking, Chopra says. “When defensive protocols are codified into the architecture rather than enforced by a review board, engineering teams can maintain high developer velocity while inherently restricting the attack surface.” It transforms security from a workflow tax into an automated platform capability, he states. 5. Beware bureaucracy that does not lead to decisive action Stop treating your security strategy as an annual document process and begin viewing it as a loop that runs continuously utilizing data you trust, says Bob Maley, CISO at security-as-a-service provider Black Kite. Feed decisions to someone who actually has the authority to make rapid critical choices, he recommends. Attackers are already highly vigilant, Maley warns. “When a new vulnerability opportunity lands on a Friday afternoon, nobody on a ransomware crew is waiting for a quarterly review to approve going after it,” he explains. “If your defense team needs a steering committee before it can react, the gap between their tempo and yours is where the breach lives.” 6. Embrace automation to free up human judgment Most security teams I’ve worked with build static defenses, observes Timur Rakhmatullin, senior software engineer at Softline Solutions, a consulting and social media marketing services provider. “They set up rules, configure alerts, and write runbooks, but then something happens that doesn’t match the runbook and everyone freezes.” Rakhmatullin believes that automation is essential. He runs automated security scans across 30-plus repositories using in-house tools. “The scans catch vulnerabilities, license issues, and other gaps,” Rakhmatullin explains. “But the key part is that any engineer can override a scan result, escalate it, or reclassify a finding in minutes.” Still, automation does all the heavy lifting, Rakhmatullin says. “Humans make the judgment calls.” 7. Conduct regular ‘fire drills’ Rehearse ugly scenarios before they happen, suggests Chris McGlasson, founder of ClearStack Advisory, a fractional executive technology and AI strategy firm. Know who patches, who tests, who talks to the business, and who has the authority to take something offline at 2 a.m., McGlasson says. “Write it down and run it twice a year,” he recommends. “The teams that do so treat incident response like a fire drill.” McGlasson adds that many CISOs risk disaster because they treat security like a research project instead of a fundamental initiative. McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of critical zero-day exploits . Citrix immediately warned IT administrators to patch their systems at once to address the issue. As a result, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, gave federal agencies a three-day patch window, while other organizations were left to create their own timeline, McGlasson says. He notes that the shops that handled this challenging event well weren’t always the ones with the best tools. “They were the ones that already knew who patches, who tests, and who calls the shots before the advisory ever dropped.” Agility is a muscle, McGlasson observes. “You build it through repetition.”
